title: A Migrating Bird's Wings Trade Speed for Sharp Turns
summary:
The European nightjar is a bird that hunts insects at night. Every year, it migrates thousands of miles between Europe and southern Africa. You might expect a bird that travels so far to have wings built for fast, efficient flying. But scientists have found that the nightjar's wings make a trade-off.

Researchers at Lund University studied nightjars in a wind tunnel. They recorded how the birds moved at different speeds and measured the patterns of air left behind their wings.

The nightjar has broad wing tips. These likely help it make sharp turns while flying slowly to catch insects. But at higher speeds, the broad tips become a disadvantage, and the wings make lift less efficiently. Lift is the force that helps keep a bird in the air.

"Instead, the nightjar's wings appear to be a compromise between several different demands," says Christoffer Johansson, a scientist at Lund University.

The team also found a surprise. Even as the nightjar raises its wings, during the part of the wingbeat called the upstroke, it keeps creating thrust. Thrust is the force that moves it forward. This is unusual, because an active upstroke like this has mainly been linked to bats and insects, not birds.

The finding suggests that very different animals may have found similar ways to solve the problems of flying.

The discovery could also help engineers. Drones and robots with flapping wings may face limits on how much their wings can fold during each beat. Learning how nightjars push forward on the upstroke could help such machines fly better.

Next, the researchers want to find out whether other birds and flying animals use the same trick, or whether it is special to the nightjar.
why_it_matters: The study shows that evolution often balances competing needs instead of perfecting one, and nature's solutions can inspire new flying machines.
